https://english.radio.cz/osoblazka-a-nar.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Osoblažka: A narrow-gauge railway through a magical corner of Czechia, straight out of a fairy-tale Facebook Twitter It's one of Czechia's best-kept secrets: a narrow-gauge railway that snakes through a fairy-tale landscape in the country's far northeast. We took a ride on the Osoblažka to find out what makes it so special. All aboard! Finding Osoblaha on a map of Czechia is no easy task. The village of around one thousand people lies in a former Moravian enclave within Silesia. Nearly destroyed during the final battles of World War II and later affected by the expulsion of its German population, the region became one of the country's most remote corners - geographically and in the public’s imagination. Yet today, its historic narrow-gauge railway has turned it into an unforgettable summer destination. Wait for the green light! "If you're travelling with us for the first time, please don't touch the door handle until the green light comes on!" Driver Lukáš Weiss reminds the passengers before the last Friday evening train departs from Třemešná on its winding 20-kilometre journey to Osoblaha. Although the railway's vintage carriages are decades old, safety has improved significantly, including locking the old-style door handles while the train is moving. Once everyone is aboard, Lukáš rushes to the locomotive. His shift begins early in the morning and doesn't end until after he spends the night at Osoblaha station and drives the first train back the following day. "I’m not looking too good," he says. Standing in the sweltering locomotive cab, he smiles apologetically at the sweat soaking through his red uniform shirt. As the train rolls through the countryside, he points out the wildlife outside. "There's a roe deer running on the left, but that's a fallow deer on the right! We often see cranes here too. It's beautiful around here." A railway revived the region The Osoblaha region remains refreshingly untouched: no crowds, no teeming car parks, no overpriced ice cream or tourist traps. Visitors are welcomed by a more serene life. They may find a unique Jewish cemetery, a regional museum, and the Osoblažka itself - a narrow-gauge railway that has been running since December 1898. Nicknamed the "Railway of One Hundred Tuns," it actually winds through even more bends than that. More than just a tourist-train For local resident Anna Žigová, travelling home with her three granddaughters from Krnov, the train is part of everyday life. "Sometimes we take the bus, sometimes the train, but this is much better for the children," she says as the girls watch the countryside pass by in the evening sun. The railway brings together locals, commuters, tourists, railway enthusiasts and families. On board, passengers can even buy refreshments. "Would you like a coffee with a wafer? Or perhaps a non-alcoholic beer?" steward Michal Majetny asks as he walks through the train; a pleasant and unexpected service on such a small regional railway. A labour of love "Where do all the passengers come from?" conductor Roman Vrábel ponders. "During the school year it's children going to school and people commuting to work. In summer there are mainly tourists. And when the steam train is running, some people travel one way on the steam service and return on this diesel train." Roman normally works as a dispatcher at Ostrava's main railway station, but spends his free time working on the Osoblažka. "Yes, I earn a little extra, but above all I enjoy it. I like people." His new colleague Rostislav is making an even bigger career change, leaving teaching behind to train as a locomotive driver after moving into Bohušov station. Meanwhile, the volunteers running the historic steam trains and those operating the regular passenger service work seamlessly together. "When the organisation decided to take over regular passenger services from Czech Railways for local people and tourists, they simply asked those of us working on the steam trains whether we'd join them," says operations manager Pavel Schreier, who is spending the day shovelling ash from a steam locomotive. "The answer was obvious." Like the peaceful countryside it passes through, the Osoblažka has a quiet charm of its own. Free from crowds and commercial attractions, this little railway has become one of Czechia's most beautiful and unique summer journeys. https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/mi.text: A Ryanair passenger said he thought he was 'going to die' as passengers prayed for their lives on 'the worst flight ever' to Birmingham Airport. Connor Horton said other travellers were "screaming and crying" and some were praying when his flight from Krakow in Poland hit turbulence on Thursday, July 23. The 25-year-old, who is a Sandwell Labour councillor covering Great Barr, Yew Tree and Tamebridge, said his journey had already been delayed by a thunderstorm before the turbulence hit. READ MORE: 'They do not represent my town' says Halesowen local after 'frightening' High Street brawl He told BirminghamLive: "People were screaming, someone was crying, the whole thing was awful. "It was only a two-hour flight and it felt like it went on. There were times when we had aggressive drops and it would shoot back up. "That's when people were getting upset and scared, I was terrified. "The sensation was awful and the whole plane was panicking. I thought 'what the f**k is going on?' and that's when I saw people praying. "It just didn't seem normal. I've never been on a flight like that. It was the worst flight of my life and I've flown across the Atlantic, the Caribbean, it was the worst one ever. "We were operated by Ryanair but it was a Polish crew and I couldn't understand their accents. We were told we would arrive early, but I'm sure we arrived ten minutes late. "Everyone clapped and sighed in relief when it landed in Birmingham. "I had never flown with Ryanair and the flight to Kraków shook me up when it landed aggressively." A Ryanair spokesperson said: “This flight from Krakow to Birmingham experienced some minor air turbulence shortly before landing at Birmingham Airport.”

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn5n.text: Image gallery Skip image gallery Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The 55.6-metre (182ft) concrete figure is nearly 18m taller than Rio de Janeiro's Christ the Redeemer Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Bishop Krzysztof WÄtkowski, who consecrated the statue, said "many contemporary people look only to the earth" Image source, EPA Image caption, The statue's consecration was chosen to coincide with the Feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary 1 of 3 Previous image Next image Slide 1 of 3 , A statue of the Virgin Mary rises out of green and yellow fields in Poland on a cloudy sky. , The 55.6-metre (182ft) concrete figure is nearly 18m taller than Rio de Janeiro's Christ the Redeemer End of image gallery By Aleks Phillips Published 55 minutes ago A statue of the Virgin Mary believed to be Europe's tallest has been formally unveiled in a small Polish village. The 55.6-metre (182ft) concrete figure is roughly two double-decker buses longer than Rio de Janeiro's smaller - if more prominently placed - Christ the Redeemer monument, though it still pales in comparison to a 98m Virgin Mary erected in the Philippines. The ecclesiastical sculpture in rural Konotopie was consecrated by a local bishop in a ceremony on Saturday, a day chosen to coincide with the Feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Its inauguration comes at a time when the influence of the Catholic church on public life in Poland has declined. The icon's remote location - in a field miles from any of Poland's population centres - is largely due to it being commissioned by a millionaire couple who live locally. Two helicopters circled to drop rose petals over the Virgin Mary, which stands in a large crown with open arms, during Saturday's ceremony. Bishop Krzysztof WÄtkowski, who consecrated the statue, told those congregated that "many contemporary people look only to the earth, focused on themselves", whereas the figure beckoned "to raise our gaze upwards to God and heaven", according to Polish news agency PAP. While Poland remains an overwhelmingly Catholic country, many younger Poles in urban areas have increasingly turned away from the church and its traditions. Among the attendees on Saturday was Lech WaÅÄsa, who led the movement to end communism in Poland and would go on to become the country's first democratically elected president. WaÅÄsa famously wore a Virgin Mary pin badge while campaigning and credited his Catholic faith as playing a major role in his fight against communism. "I started with the Virgin Mary and I end with the Virgin Mary," the 82-year-old told the Associated Press. https://www.travelwires.com/campanile-pr.text: Campanile PRIME and Première Classe open dual-brand hotel hub near Warsaw Chopin Airport Published by Maisha Swanson on August 26, 2026 in Hotels & Resorts • 4 min read Louvre Hotels Group and Sangate Sancak have opened a new dual-brand hotel complex near Warsaw Chopin Airport, bringing together Campanile PRIME and Première Classe under one development. The new hotel hub welcomed its first guests on June 9, 2026, and is located on Komitet Obrony Robotników Street, approximately 1.5 kilometres from Warsaw’s main international airport. Together, the two hotels provide 391 rooms across different price points, targeting business travellers, leisure guests and passengers requiring accommodation before an early departure, after a late arrival or during a stopover in Warsaw. The project represents another step in the long-term partnership between Louvre Hotels Group and Sangate Sancak in Poland. Campanile PRIME Warsaw Airport opens with 223 rooms The larger of the two properties is Campanile PRIME Warsaw Airport, offering 223 rooms and a more elevated version of the traditional Campanile experience. Louvre Hotels Group is gradually introducing the PRIME concept across Poland as part of an upgrade of the Campanile brand, combining its midscale positioning with higher standards in rooms, communal areas and services. Guestrooms at the Warsaw Airport property feature 30-centimetre mattresses, 100% cotton textiles, free high-speed Wi-Fi and Chromecast connectivity. Fitness kits are also available for guests who want to exercise in their rooms, reflecting the property’s focus on frequent and business travellers. “The PRIME concept sets a new direction in the development of one of our most popular brands,” said François Delattre, Vice President International Operations Europe at Louvre Hotels Group. “This is a response to the changing expectations of guests who are looking for not only accommodation but a coherent experience in which comfort comes first, but the best quality-price ratio is also important.” Coworking and conference facilities target business travellers Communal spaces form a significant part of the Campanile PRIME concept. The new hotel includes multifunctional lobby areas and coworking spaces designed to accommodate work, informal meetings and relaxation throughout the day. Food and beverage facilities follow a city-bistro format, with seasonal menus and breakfast options incorporating locally sourced products. Campanile PRIME Warsaw Airport also includes around 800 square metres of conference and event space, supported by catering services. Its proximity to both the airport and Warsaw city centre is expected to make the property particularly relevant for corporate meetings and travellers visiting the Polish capital for business. Première Classe adds 168 affordable rooms The second hotel in the development, Première Classe Warsaw Airport, targets travellers looking for a more affordable and straightforward stay. The hotel offers 168 rooms in double, twin and triple configurations. While the concept is more limited-service than Campanile PRIME, Louvre Hotels Group says the property maintains a focus on comfortable beds, efficient service and convenient transport connections. The combination allows the same hotel complex to serve guests with different budgets without requiring separate locations or infrastructure. Both hotels also participate in Louvre Hotels Group’s established Pet Friendly programme in Poland, allowing travellers to stay with their pets. Louvre Hotels Group expands dual-brand strategy in Poland The Warsaw Airport project is not the company’s first multi-brand development in Poland. Louvre Hotels Group already operates Campanile and Première Classe hotels together on Ślężna Street in Wrocław. In central Warsaw, the group has another hotel hub on Towarowa Street combining Campanile PRIME and Première Classe with Golden Tulip, its upscale brand. The company also operates Golden Tulip Warsaw Airport near Chopin Airport. With the addition of Campanile PRIME and Première Classe, Louvre Hotels Group can now offer accommodation across several price segments in the immediate airport area. “The two-brand hub at Chopin Airport implements a model that we have already tested in our owned portfolio,” Delattre said. “With the opening of the new Campanile PRIME and Première Classe addresses, we will offer travelers almost the full spectrum of Louvre Hotels Group experiences: from one to four stars.” Airport hotel market continues to diversify The new development reflects a broader hotel strategy of combining multiple brands within a single complex to serve different traveller profiles while sharing infrastructure and operational resources. For airport locations in particular, demand can range from budget-conscious passengers requiring a short overnight stay to corporate travellers looking for meeting facilities, restaurants and additional services. Campanile PRIME Warsaw Airport and Première Classe Warsaw Airport address both ends of that spectrum while benefiting from their location close to Poland’s busiest airport. Louvre Hotels Group currently operates more than 1,750 hotels across 70 countries, with brands ranging from Première Classe and Campanile to Golden Tulip and Royal Tulip. https://hungarytoday.hu/record-low-danub.text: Record-Low Danube Forces Emergency Measures at Budapest’s Oldest Power Plant The record-low water level of the Danube has created operational challenges for the Kelenföld Power Plant, Budapest’s oldest municipal power plant. To ensure its water supply, the plant’s specialists dredged part of the nearby Lágymányosi Bay, spending HUF 20 million (EUR 55,000) to prevent a potential emergency, the Budapest Power Plant Company (BERT), part of the Veolia Group, told MTI . The specialists prepared the work in just two days and, during the first week of August, deepened a 50-meter section of the bay by 50 to 100 centimeters. The dredging was carried out using appropriate technology and in accordance with legal requirements, the company emphasized. Kelenföld Power Plant. Photo: MTI /Szigetváry Zsolt Around 300 to 400 cubic meters of sediment were removed and spread along the shoreline. In the power plant’s more than 110-year history, this was the first time dredging had been necessary to safeguard operations while preserving the bay’s ecosystem. The Kelenföld Power Plant draws the water needed for electricity generation from Lágymányosi Bay. A continuous supply of cooling and raw water is essential for the safe and uninterrupted operation of its equipment. Without it, serious disruptions could occur, potentially affecting electricity generation. Plant specialists therefore faced a dual challenge: preventing an operational emergency caused by the Danube’s exceptionally low water level, while maintaining uninterrupted electricity production at a time when extreme heat had driven up nationwide demand for power. During the summer, the plant supplies hot water to nearly 41,000 households and 1,800 public institutions, while in winter it also provides district heating. Hot-water service to residents remained uninterrupted throughout the summer, and measures were taken during the dredging work to ensure that noise did not disturb people living or working nearby. The company said the emergency measures also helped protect the bay’s ecosystem. Continuous water extraction creates circulation that naturally replaces and oxygenates the otherwise stagnant water, helping preserve aquatic life in the bay. Fact On September 8, the Danube fell to its lowest recorded level in Budapest after continuing to decline throughout the summer. The official gauge showed just one centimeter above its reference point. The record-low reading may sound alarming, but it does not mean the Danube is only one centimeter deep in Budapest. Gabriella Siklós, spokesperson for the National Water Directorate, told MTI that the river is actually about 3 to 3.5 meters deep on average in Budapest, but water levels this low are already preventing some larger vessels from navigating the river. The Danube at a record low at the Vigadó Square gauge in Budapest on September 9, 2026. Photo: MT I/Máthé Zoltán The one-centimeter reading means the water surface is just one centimeter above the artificially established zero point of the Budapest gauge. That reference level was set in the 19th century. Due to river regulation, the lowering of the riverbed and increasingly frequent droughts, the Danube has fallen below the 19th-century minimum levels in recent decades. The river’s previous record low in Budapest was 28 centimeters, recorded at the end of July 2026. Authorities are expecting water levels to rise over the weekend, as meteorologists are forecasting significant rainfall in the upper reaches of the Danube. Bomb disposal teams report nearly 70% more discoveries, with the Danube accounting for more than half of recent reports. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon who has denied murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024. Photograph: Rocco Fazzari/AAP View image in fullscreen A court sketch of Beau Lamarre-Condon who has denied murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in early 2024. Photograph: Rocco Fazzari/AAP New South Wales Beau Lamarre-Condon asked police investigator about murder of Lilie James day before shootings, court hears Lamarre-Condon asked fellow officer if Paul Thijssen ‘would have gotten away with’ James’s murder if he hadn’t subsequently killed himself Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Kat Wong Thu 1 Oct 2026 22.04 EDT Last modified on Thu 1 Oct 2026 22.08 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon asked a colleague, a day before he allegedly murdered Jesse Baird and Luke Davies, if a high-profile killer would have “gotten away with it” if he’d not taken his own life, a Sydney court has heard. Lamarre-Condon, 31, has been accused of fatally shooting the couple with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024. He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter. Ben Higginson, who served with the New South Wales police force criminal investigation team in Sydney, told the supreme court trial on Friday about working with Lamarre-Condon the day before Baird and Davies were killed. ‘Don’t freak out’: Beau Lamarre-Condon asked friend if hire cars could be tracked before alleged murders, court hears Read more The two police officers had been working at a pro-Palestine protest on 18 February 2024 when Lamarre-Condon asked Higginson about work. Higginson replied that it had been a “bit of a rough time” as he had been investigating the murder of Lilie James . James, 21, was a water polo coach at St Andrew’s Cathedral school who was killed by Paul Thijssen in October 2023 days after the pair broke up. CCTV captured Thijssen following James into the school’s gymnasium with a hammer before her body was found. He later killed himself at the Vaucluse cliffs. View image in fullscreen Lilie James was murdered in October 2023. Photograph: Lilie James/Facebook Higginson became emotional when discussing the case with Lamarre-Condon, noting the crime had occurred at his old school, so it “hit home a bit more”, the court was told on Friday. But when Lamarre-Condon asked about James’s murder he seemed “blase”, Higginson told the court. “He thought Paul was stupid for doing it on CCTV,” the police investigator said. Higginson told the court that Lamarre-Condon then asked if Thijssen hadn’t committed suicide “would he have gotten away with it?” The investigator said police didn’t only rely on CCTV when examining a crime. Higginson brought up the 2007 death of Matthew Leveson and told Lamarre-Condon he “could remember the CCTV of [Leveson’s] partner at Bunnings buying tarp, and he ended up burying him in the national park”. Both police officers then spoke about how cash was more difficult to trace than bank cards and “what avenues detectives look at for suspicious deaths”, the court heard. When Lamarre-Condon asked about phones, Higginson said he responded: “If you were to leave your phone at home and commit a murder, the phone would be showing up in the vicinity of your residence.” Higginson said the two weren’t close, but they would chat at work, and he recalled Lamarre-Condon would tell him about his “side-hustles”. “Apparently he goes to France to buy Hermes bags and resell them here,” he told the court. The defence lawyer John Stratton SC said during his opening statement that Baird and Davies were fatally shot in “self-defence” after struggles with the policeman. Lamarre-Condon immediately began cleaning up the scene because he “panicked”, the jury was told. The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues. https://albaniandailynews.com/news/railw.text: Home Politics Economy Current Events Op-Ed Social Sport Region World News Contact Durrës railway station Share Tweet Railway Reform, Albania Last in the Region Economy Thursday, September 24, 2026 Albania has slowed the pace of railway sector reform in 2025 and remains the country with the lowest level of implementation regarding the Western Balkans Regional Railway Reform Plan. According to the "2025 Report on the Implementation of the Green Agenda for the Western Balkans Action Plan," Albania's railway reform implementation fell to 45% in 2025, down from 51% in 2024. Bosnia and Herzegovina was at 52%, Montenegro at 60%, Kosova and North Macedonia at 62% each, and Serbia at 65%. Serbia also recorded a sharp decline, down from 93% in 2024. One element of the reform is the opening of the railway market to operators. On this indicator, Albania is rated at 52%, compared to 89% for Serbia, 67% for Kosova and North Macedonia, 56% for Montenegro, and 40% for Bosnia and Herzegovina. Another issue is the pace of infrastructure modernization. Work continues in Albania to connect Tirana Airport to the railway network as part of the Tirana-Durrës line. The report also mentions preparatory work to connect Porto Romano and Vlora to the road and railway networks. However, the report assesses that, despite these projects, the overall pace of constructing multimodal terminals and modernizing road and rail infrastructure in the region remains relatively slow. Part of the reform specifically concerns establishing connections between railways, ports, airports, and road transport, enabling goods to transfer more easily from one mode of transport to another. In this regard, Albania has not yet transposed European rules on combined freight transport. The report notes that only Serbia and Montenegro have partially transposed these rules, whereas other countries in the region have not. Another weakness of the reform in the region concerns cross-border rail crossings. The report observes that activities planned for 2025 in this area have shown little to no progress across most of the Western Balkans, with the exception of some developments between Serbia and Hungary. The other countries failed to make significant progress in establishing a legal framework for joint rail border checks, setting up joint stations, or renovating cross-border rail lines. Albania shows a relatively low level of alignment between its domestic regulations and the European railway system.
